description: I’m a London-based participant for NASA Space Apps 2026, currently solo and open to new teammates. I handle research, development, design, and project coordination. My interests include space exploration, astrophysics, Earth observation, and sustainability. I’m looking for teammates — especially those with astrophysics, data, coding, or science expertise. Commitment matters most. Let’s collaborate and build something meaningful together.
summary:
FieldShift is a web app that helps farmers choose crop rotations that protect soil, save water and cope with a changing climate. A farmer clicks their field on a satellite map, enters their current rotation and sets their priorities: water, soil nitrogen, erosion, organic matter, pest control, income or forage.

FieldShift then combines 25 years of NASA POWER climate data (including GPM IMERG rainfall and soil moisture) with MODIS vegetation, SRTM terrain, USDA soil and cropland data, and ERA5 as a cross-check. It works out frost seasons, heat stress, water balance, bare-soil months and statistically tested long-term trends. Its rotation engine scores 26 crops and cover crops and evaluates over 1,000 rotations. It compares the farmer’s current rotation with three alternatives, explaining for each why it was suggested, the evidence, the benefits, the information gaps and the risks to check locally.

This matters because rotation choices shape soil health and food security for years, yet farmers rarely see satellite data in a usable form. FieldShift turns that data into clear, honest options that support, not replace, farmer judgment.
details:
FieldShift is a decision-support web app that helps farmers explore crop rotations suited to their field and a changing climate. The farmer clicks their field on a satellite map. For US fields, FieldShift reads the field’s real crop history from the USDA Cropland Data Layer and can auto-fill the current rotation. The farmer then sets priorities (saving water, soil nitrogen, erosion control, organic matter, pest-cycle breaks, income or forage) and can test climate scenarios such as +2 °C and −20% rain.

The backend fetches data from six sources in parallel:

  • NASA POWER: 25 years of daily temperature, GPM IMERG-corrected rainfall and soil moisture.
  • MODIS NDVI: vegetation greenness.
  • SRTM: elevation, used for slope and erosion zones.
  • USDA SSURGO / ISRIC SoilGrids: soil properties.
  • USDA Cropland Data Layer: field crop history and crops grown nearby.
  • ERA5: an independent climate record used to cross-check NASA POWER.

From this data it works out frost-free seasons, growing degree days, heat and frost days, evapotranspiration, water balance and Mann-Kendall trend tests. It scores 26 crops and cover crops for suitability. Then it builds over 1,000 possible rotations, fills bare-soil months with cover crops and ranks them on eight measures weighted by the farmer’s priorities. The result is the farmer’s current rotation alongside three distinct alternatives, each explained with why it was suggested, the evidence, the benefits, the information gaps and the risks to check locally.

What benefits does it have?

  • Turns complex satellite and climate data into plain-language options a farmer can act on.
  • Shows hidden problems, such as soil left bare during heavy-rain months, rising heat stress or drying trends.
  • Explains its reasoning with specific numbers, so recommendations can be checked rather than taken on trust.
  • Rates its own data confidence by comparing two independent climate sources.
  • Flags new crops nobody grows nearby, so farmers confirm a buyer before planting.
  • Free data, no accounts or API keys, and an offline demo mode.

What is the intended impact?

We want farmers, agronomists and extension advisers to make faster, better-informed rotation decisions that improve soil health, reduce water use and erosion, and build resilience to climate change. It also has an educational role: students and the public can see how NASA Earth observations connect to food production.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did you use?

  • Backend: Python with FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, httpx, NumPy and SciPy; pytest for automated tests.
  • Frontend: JavaScript with React 18 and Vite, Leaflet for the map, Chart.js for charts, and CSS.
  • Data access: the NASA POWER, ORNL DAAC MODIS, USDA Soil Data Access, ISRIC SoilGrids, OpenTopoData (SRTM), USDA CropScape and Open-Meteo (ERA5) web services.
  • Optional AI: the Anthropic Claude API writes a plain-English summary using only the computed results.
  • Development: VS Code and Git. Hardware: standard laptops; no special hardware needed.

How is the project creative?

  • Field calendar: a month-by-month view showing what covers the soil and flagging erosion, heat, frost and drought risk.
  • Auto-filled rotations: USDA crop history fills in the farmer’s real rotation from satellite classification.
  • Market signal from space: crops grown nearby, seen in satellite cropland data, stand in for local markets and know-how.
  • Self-checking data: ERA5 is used to rate how far the NASA POWER climate figures can be trusted.
  • Automatic cover crops: bare windows are filled using agronomic rules, such as a legume before a nitrogen-hungry crop.
  • Climate scenarios: “what if” sliders show which rotations hold up as conditions change.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Farmer-centred design: plain language, a glossary, few inputs and clear visuals for users with limited technical background.
  • Honesty about uncertainty: data resolution, cross-source agreement and information gaps are shown, and every option ends with “review with a local adviser”.
  • Supporting, not replacing, judgment: scores are relative comparisons, not yield or profit predictions.
  • Practicality: a penalty for adding unfamiliar crops, plus equipment, buyer and herbicide carry-over warnings.
  • Global reach: works worldwide and flips seasons for the Southern Hemisphere; US-only datasets switch off gracefully elsewhere.
  • Reliability: every data source fails safely, downloads are cached, and an offline demo mode copes with poor connectivity.
  • Accessibility: colour-blind-safe chart colours, dark mode, keyboard navigation and table views for charts.
  • Openness: only free, public datasets, so anyone can use and extend the tool.
